title: The birthday problem
objectives: Compute the chance that two people in a room share a birthday.
Explain why the number of pairs makes the chance grow fast.

screens.title: A six-day year
screens.prose: Picture a planet whose year has 6 days, each equally likely as a birthday. Two people meet. Each cell is one pair of birthdays.
screens.question: Tap every cell where the two people share a birthday.

hints.text: A shared birthday means both people have the same day. Which cells are (3, 3) and its kind?
The matches lie on one diagonal, from the top left corner.
Tap (1, 1), (2, 2) and so on up to (6, 6).

feedback.correct: Six of the 36 cells are matches: a chance of $\tfrac{1}{6}$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A match is a cell whose two days are equal, and there is one for every day.

byKey.one-day: Day 1 is one way to match. Any of the 6 days can be the shared one.

explain.text: The matches are the 6 cells on the diagonal, so two people share with chance $\tfrac{6}{36} = \tfrac{1}{6}$. Whatever the first person's day, the second matches it with chance $\tfrac{1}{6}$. In a 365-day year that is $\tfrac{1}{365}$.

screens.prose: A third person joins, still in the six-day year. Person 2 avoids person 1's day with chance $\tfrac{5}{6}$. Then person 3 must avoid two taken days.

state.caption: Six-day year: each person either lands on a new day or shares

screens.question: What is the chance at least two of the three share a birthday?

hints.text: It is easier to find the chance that all three birthdays differ.
All different means the path New day, then New day.
$\tfrac{5}{6} \times \tfrac{4}{6} = \tfrac{20}{36}$ for all different. Take that from 1.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the chance all three differ along the tree, then use the complement.

byKey.pairs-added: You added $\tfrac{1}{6}$ for each of the 3 pairs. The pairs overlap, so adding counts some outcomes twice.
byKey.one-day: You let person 3 avoid only one day. Two days are taken by then, so the chance is $\tfrac{4}{6}$.
byKey.all-diff: $\tfrac{5}{9}$ is the chance all three differ. You want the other side.

explain.text: All different needs New day twice: $\tfrac{5}{6} \cdot \tfrac{4}{6} = \tfrac{20}{36}$. Each factor counts the days still free. So a shared birthday has chance $1 - \tfrac{20}{36} = \tfrac{4}{9}$.

screens.prose: Now a real year of 365 days. Each new person must avoid every day already taken: $$P(\text{no shared}) = \frac{365}{365} \cdot \frac{364}{365} \cdot \frac{363}{365} \cdots$$ with one factor per person. The curve plots 1 minus that product. Move the slider.

screens.title: Why intuition fails
screens.prose: Intuition compares 23 people with 365 days. But a match can happen between any two people in the room, not just between you and someone else.
screens.question: How many different pairs of people are there among 23?

hints.text: Each pair is a choice of 2 people from 23, where order does not matter.
Use $\binom{23}{2}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Choose 2 of the 23 people, and do not count a pair twice.

byKey.people: That counts people. Matches happen between pairs of people.
byKey.others: 22 is the number of pairs that include you. Other pairs can match too.
byKey.ordered: You counted each pair twice, as (Ann, Ben) and (Ben, Ann). Divide by 2.

explain.text: There are $\binom{23}{2} = 253$ pairs, each a 1 in 365 chance of a match. Pairs grow like $\tfrac{n^2}{2}$, so they outrun the people fast. The pairs overlap, so we use the product, not a sum.

screens.prose: You join a room of 23 other people. Two questions sound alike. Will one of them share **your** birthday? Will any two of those 23 share one?
screens.question: What is the chance that at least two of the 23 share a birthday?

options.why: You divided 23 by 365. That ignores the 253 pairs, and it is not the chance of any event here.
That is $1 - (\tfrac{364}{365})^{23}$, the chance someone shares **your** birthday. Any of the 253 pairs can match, not only pairs with you.
You added $\tfrac{1}{365}$ for each of the 253 pairs. The pairs overlap, so adding counts outcomes more than once.

hints.text: Is this about your birthday, or any pair at all?
Read the curve at 23.
Any pair counts, so use the product: $1 - \prod_{i=0}^{22} \tfrac{365 - i}{365}$.

feedback.correct: 0.5073: any of the 253 pairs may match.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The question allows any two of the 23 to match.

byKey.you: That is $1 - (\tfrac{364}{365})^{23}$, the chance someone shares **your** birthday. Any of the 253 pairs can match, not only pairs with you.

explain.text: Someone matching you has chance $1 - (\tfrac{364}{365})^{23} = 0.0612$, the dashed curve. Any two of the 23 matching has chance 0.5073. The first question uses 23 pairs; the second uses 253.

screens.prose: Write the product out in general. Assume 365 equally likely days, no leap day, and birthdays that do not depend on each other. Add people one at a time.
screens.question: Put the lines of the derivation in order.

lines.text: Person 1 can have any birthday: chance $\tfrac{365}{365}$.
Person 2 must avoid 1 taken day: chance $\tfrac{364}{365}$.
Person $i + 1$ must avoid the $i$ taken days: chance $\tfrac{365 - i}{365}$.
Each factor is given the ones before, so multiply: $P(\text{no shared}) = \prod_{i=0}^{n-1} \tfrac{365 - i}{365}$.

hints.text: Start with the first person, who cannot clash with anyone.
The general line for person $i + 1$ comes after the two examples.
People one by one, then the product, then the complement.

feedback.correct: One factor per person, multiplied, then the complement.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add people in order, multiply, and only then take the complement.

byKey.s5: The complement needs the full product first, so it comes last.

explain.text: Each line adds one person and counts the days still free. Multiplying is the rule for stages, each given the last. The complement turns “no shared birthday” into “at least one shared”.

screens.title: The product in code
screens.prose: Turn the product into a function. Loop over the people, multiply in each new factor, then take the complement. Use only plain Python.

screens.title: Certain at last
screens.prose: At 70 people the chance is 0.9992: close to certain, but not certain. Some room size makes a shared birthday a sure thing.
screens.question: What is the smallest number of people that guarantees a shared birthday?

hints.text: Could 365 people all have different birthdays?
With 365 people, every day could be used exactly once.
The next person has nowhere new to go: 366.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the first room where different birthdays run out of days.

byKey.days: 365 people can still all differ, one per day. One more person forces a match.
byKey.half: 183 already makes a match almost certain, but not certain.
byKey.seventy: At 70 the chance is 0.9992, not 1. Different birthdays are still possible.

explain.text: With 365 people every day can be used once, so no match is forced. Person 366 has no free day: the factor $\tfrac{365 - 365}{365} = 0$ makes the product 0. This is the pigeonhole principle.

screens.prose: A strategy sends 30 trades in one minute. The log stamps each trade to the second, so there are 60 possible stamps. Treat each stamp as equally likely and independent.
screens.question: What is the chance at least two of the 30 trades share a timestamp?

options.why: You divided 30 by 60. That ignores the 435 pairs of trades.
That is the birthday answer for 30 people and 365 days. Here there are only 60 seconds.
That is $1 - (\tfrac{59}{60})^{29}$, the chance some trade shares a second with one given trade.

hints.text: This is the birthday problem with 60 days and 30 people.
$P(\text{no shared}) = \prod_{i=0}^{29} \tfrac{60 - i}{60}$.
Ten trades already give 0.5475. Thirty trades leave almost no room.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use the product with 60 slots and 30 trades.

byKey.one-trade: That is the chance some trade shares a second with one given trade. Any of the 435 pairs can match.

explain.text: With 60 slots the chance passes a half at just 10 trades, 0.5475. At 30 trades it is 0.99986. A timestamp alone will almost never identify a trade, so logs need a sequence number too.

screens.prose: A small broker tags each order with a random 4-digit code, so 10,000 codes are possible. It sends 100 orders a day. Two orders with the same code would clash.
screens.question: What is the chance of at least one clash in a day of 100 orders?

options.why: You divided 100 by 10,000. That ignores the 4,950 pairs.
That is the chance some order clashes with one given order. Any pair can clash.
You added $\tfrac{1}{10000}$ for each of the 4,950 pairs. The pairs overlap, so the sum overcounts.

hints.text: This is the birthday problem with 10,000 days and 100 people.
The pair count, 4,950, is near half of 10,000, so expect a chance well above 1%.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use the birthday product with 10,000 codes.

byKey.summed: You added $\tfrac{1}{10000}$ for each of the 4,950 pairs. The pairs overlap, so the sum overcounts.

explain.text: The product gives 0.3914, about 2 days in 5. Collisions arrive near $\sqrt{10000} = 100$ draws, not 10,000. Hash tables and order systems size their codes with this in mind.

ideas: Find the chance that nobody shares, one person at a time, then take the complement.
With $n$ people there are $\binom{n}{2}$ pairs, and pairs grow like $\tfrac{n^2}{2}$. That is why 23 people already pass one half.
With $d$ equally likely slots, collisions arrive after about $\sqrt{d}$ draws, not $d$.

formula.name: Shared birthday among $n$ people
formula.note: 23 people give 0.5073, 50 give 0.9704, 70 give 0.9992; 366 make it certain.

summary.trap: $1 - (\tfrac{364}{365})^n$ is the chance someone shares **your** birthday. Any pair can match, so the true chance is far higher.

quiz.question: How many pairs of people could share a birthday?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Choose 2 of the 30, without order.

byKey.ordered: You counted each pair twice, once in each order.
byKey.others: 29 is the number of pairs including one person. Count every pair.

explain.text: A pair is 2 people chosen from 30 without order: $\tfrac{30 \times 29}{2} = 435$. So 30 people make 435 chances of a match.

quiz.question: What is the chance that at least two of them show the same number?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the chance all four differ first.

byKey.pairs: You added $\tfrac{1}{6}$ for each of the 6 pairs and got 1. Pairs overlap, so that overcounts.
byKey.one-die: That is $1 - (\tfrac{5}{6})^3$, a match with the first die only.
byKey.all-diff: That is the chance all four differ. Take it from 1.

explain.text: All different has chance $\tfrac{6}{6} \cdot \tfrac{5}{6} \cdot \tfrac{4}{6} \cdot \tfrac{3}{6} = \tfrac{5}{18}$. So a repeat has chance $\tfrac{13}{18} \approx 0.7222$. It is the birthday problem with a six-day year.

quiz.question: What is the chance that some number appears at least twice?

options.why: That is the answer for 6 rolls. With 7 rolls and 6 faces, a repeat is forced.
You treated it like one pair of rolls. Seven rolls make 21 pairs.
Close, but the product has a factor $\tfrac{6 - 6}{6} = 0$, so the chance is exactly 1.

feedback.correct: Seven rolls cannot all differ with six faces.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Can seven rolls all be different?

explain.text: Six faces can be used once each in 6 rolls; the seventh must repeat one. In the product, the seventh factor is $\tfrac{6 - 6}{6} = 0$. So the chance of a repeat is exactly 1.
